name: music-theory
subject: Intervals, triads and rhythm
notes:
INTERVALS. An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in half steps. A minor third is 3 half steps and a major third is 4 half steps. A perfect fifth is 7 half steps. To name an interval, first count letter names (C up to E is a third), then count half steps to decide whether it is major or minor.

TRIADS. A triad is three notes stacked in thirds: root, third and fifth. A major triad is a major third with a minor third on top. A minor triad is a minor third with a major third on top. Both have a perfect fifth from root to top. To build a triad, start on the root, add the third, then the fifth.

CHORD PROGRESSIONS. In a major key, the I chord is home, the IV chord moves away and the V chord pulls back to I. The most common progression is I - IV - V - I. A V chord wants to resolve to I.

TIME SIGNATURES. The top number says how many beats are in a measure. The bottom number says which note value gets one beat. 4/4 has four quarter-note beats; 3/4 has three, so it feels like a waltz.

name: contract-law
subject: Contract formation
notes:
A contract needs four things: offer, acceptance, consideration and intention to create legal relations.

OFFER. An offer is a clear promise to be bound on certain terms. An advertisement is usually an invitation to treat, not an offer (Partridge v Crittenden). A shop display is also an invitation to treat (Pharmaceutical Society v Boots).

ACCEPTANCE. Acceptance must match the offer exactly. A counter-offer destroys the original offer (Hyde v Wrench). Under the postal rule, acceptance by post takes effect when the letter is posted, not when it arrives (Adams v Lindsell). Silence is not acceptance.

CONSIDERATION. Consideration is something of value given by each side. It must be sufficient but need not be adequate. Past consideration is no consideration (Re McArdle). A promise to do what you are already bound to do is not good consideration.

name: nursing-pharmacology
subject: Pharmacology for nurses
notes:
ROUTES. Intravenous drugs go straight into the blood, so bioavailability is 100 percent. Oral drugs are absorbed in the gut and pass through the liver before reaching the blood (first-pass effect), which lowers bioavailability. Sublingual drugs dissolve under the tongue and skip the liver.

HALF-LIFE. The half-life is the time for the blood concentration to fall by half. After about 5 half-lives a drug is almost completely cleared.

DOSE CALCULATION. Amount to give = (dose ordered / dose on hand) x volume or tablets on hand. Always convert units first: 1 g = 1000 mg, 1 mg = 1000 mcg. Example: ordered 500 mg, supply 250 mg per tablet, give 2 tablets. Check the answer is sensible.

DRUG CLASSES. Beta blockers (names end in -olol) slow the heart rate and lower blood pressure. ACE inhibitors (names end in -pril) lower blood pressure and can cause a dry cough. Loop diuretics such as furosemide increase urine output and can lower potassium.

name: cooking
subject: Kitchen fundamentals
notes:
KNIFE CUTS. Dice is a cube cut: large dice is 3/4 inch, medium 1/2 inch, small 1/4 inch. Julienne is a matchstick cut, about 1/8 by 1/8 by 2 inches. Brunoise is the smallest dice, 1/8 inch. Even pieces cook at the same speed. Hold the food with a claw grip so the fingertips stay behind the knuckles.

HEAT. Dry heat methods (roasting, sauteing, grilling) brown food because of the Maillard reaction, which starts above about 140 degrees C. Moist heat methods (steaming, poaching, boiling) cannot get above 100 degrees C so they do not brown. A crowded pan steams food instead of browning it. Braising means browning first, then cooking slowly in a little liquid.

SEASONING. Salt added early seasons the inside of food; salt added at the end seasons only the surface. Acid such as lemon juice brightens a dish that tastes flat. Taste and adjust before serving.

name: driving-test
subject: Driving test road rules
notes:
RIGHT OF WAY. At a four-way stop the vehicle that arrived first goes first. If two vehicles arrive at the same time, the vehicle on the right goes first. Pedestrians in a crosswalk always have right of way. A flashing red light must be treated as a stop sign. When turning left at a green light, yield to oncoming traffic.

SIGNS. Octagonal signs mean stop. Triangular signs mean yield. Yellow diamond signs warn of hazards ahead. White rectangular signs state regulations such as speed limits.

STOPPING DISTANCE. Stopping distance is reaction distance plus braking distance. Reaction distance is how far you travel before you start to brake, about 1.5 seconds. At 50 km/h total stopping distance on a dry road is about 25 metres; at 100 km/h it is about 80 metres. Doubling speed roughly quadruples the braking distance. Wet roads make braking distance much longer.

name: astronomy
subject: Astronomy
notes:
THE MOON. The Moon does not make its own light; we see the half facing the Sun. As it orbits Earth, we see different amounts of the lit half, which gives the phases: new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, then waning back to new. A full cycle takes about 29.5 days. The phases are NOT caused by Earth's shadow; Earth's shadow on the Moon causes a lunar eclipse.

STARS. A star forms when a cloud of gas and dust collapses under gravity. When the core is hot enough, hydrogen fuses into helium and the star shines for most of its life (main sequence). The Sun will swell into a red giant in about 5 billion years. A star much more massive than the Sun ends as a supernova.

PLANETS. The four inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are small and rocky. The four outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are giants. Jupiter has more than 300 times Earth's mass. Venus is hotter than Mercury because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat.

name: photosynthesis
subject: Photosynthesis
notes:
Photosynthesis turns light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose: 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + light -> C6H12O6 + 6 O2.

LIGHT REACTIONS happen in the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green, which is why leaves look green. Light energy splits water, releasing oxygen, electrons and hydrogen ions. The electrons pass along an electron transport chain, which pumps hydrogen ions across the membrane; ATP synthase uses the flow of ions back to make ATP. NADPH is also made.

THE CALVIN CYCLE happens in the stroma. The enzyme rubisco fixes carbon dioxide onto a five-carbon sugar. ATP and NADPH from the light reactions are used to turn the product into G3P, which can become glucose. Six turns of the cycle are needed for one glucose. The Calvin cycle does not use light directly.

name: spanish-preterite
subject: Spanish preterite tense
notes:
The preterite tense is used for actions that were completed in the past. Regular -ar verbs take these endings: -e, -aste, -o, -amos, -aron (hablar: hable, hablaste, hablo, hablamos, hablaron). Regular -er and -ir verbs take: -i, -iste, -io, -imos, -ieron (comer: comi, comiste, comio, comimos, comieron). The accent matters: hablo (I speak, present) is not the same as hablo with an accent on the o (he or she spoke, preterite).

Irregular verbs: ir and ser have exactly the same preterite forms: fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fueron. Tener becomes tuv-: tuve, tuviste, tuvo. Hacer becomes hic-: hice, hiciste, hizo.

Time words that signal the preterite: ayer (yesterday), anoche (last night), la semana pasada (last week), el ano pasado (last year). Example: Ayer comi pizza con mis amigos.
